1.name: GLP-1 shedding confessional — 'I finally stopped my hair falling out'
1.hook: Top-GMV variation: a woman mid-confession — 'I could scream to every single person that's on a GLP, or just losing their hair from hormones or weight' — while pouring dark softgels from the pouch into her palm with a shocked face, caption 'This DHT blocker stopped my hair fall out'; sister open is…
1.why: Identity-match ('on a GLP like me') plus a stranger's unfiltered relief lands as peer proof, and the DHT-blocker explanation gives the viewer permission to believe the fix is real. The syringe/pen prop and shed-hair overlays make the cause undeniable before the product ever appears.

1.name: Kidney warning checklist + 'nothing they can do' myth-bust (foamy-urine everyman)
1.hook: Top-GMV variation: an ordinary young man dead-serious to camera — 'These are the signs that I had and unfortunately ignored, leading to me getting diagnosed with end-stage renal disease' — under a persistent caption '5 signs that your kidneys are F*CKED', with foamy-toilet, puffy-face…
1.why: Health-scare curiosity ('signs I ignored') attached to a symptom the viewer has privately seen in the toilet turns scrolling into personal alarm. Withholding the product makes it feel like education instead of an ad, and the distrust framing ('why they tell you nothing works') positions the supplement as the answer doctors won't give.
1.sound: Suspense, horror, piano and music box — takaya

1.name: Show-the-receipts hair transformation (before/after, side-compare, inch-a-month)
1.hook: Top-GMV variation: she holds out the two sides of her hair — 'This side you can thank catching COVID three times; this side, hypothyroidism or having a kid' — caption 'I thought I was gonna be bald'.
1.why: Seeing is believing: a dramatic visible contrast (two sides, inches, baby hairs, dated before photos) is proof no claim can match. Naming the cause — COVID, thyroid, postpartum, PCOS — lets each viewer self-insert into the transformation.

1.name: 'Stop wasting money on biotin' myth-buster (hairstylist truth-teller)
1.hook: Top-GMV variation: a hairstylist points both index fingers up — 'She is completely right. As a hairstylist of 15 years...' — stacked on a shock reply-comment ('I am in complete shock! My hair stopped falling out...
1.why: Attacking what the viewer already bought (biotin, or a cheap PSO) creates instant relevance and a knowledge gap the DHT explanation resolves. The hairstylist has touched a thousand thinning heads, so her verdict feels earned rather than sold.

1.name: 'I lost half my hair' hormonal-shedding confessional + PCOS/peri symptom-stack callout
1.hook: Lead variation: 'I lost 75% of my hair in six months. And this little thing right here is what stopped it' — holding a single softgel beside her face or leaning into camera, captions like 'My secret to fast hair growth' / 'What I wish I knew before I lost 50% of it'; the cause swaps freely (grief…
1.why: A shock number ('75% in six months') from an ordinary woman plus a one-line resolution ('this little thing stopped it') is an irresistible open. The symptom-stack variant makes PCOS/peri women feel individually seen — chin hair, acne and shedding named together, which almost no ad does.

1.name: Credentialed expert explains why pumpkin seed oil works (pharmacist / researcher hook)
1.hook: Top-GMV variation: 'Why is pumpkin seed oil great for hair thinning and hair falling out?' — open-palm explainer with a university staff ID-badge overlay ('Biochem & Molecular Pharmacology'), then DHT follicle diagrams, PubMed screenshots and a finger on the 3,000mg / saw-palmetto pouch callouts.
1.why: A credential in frame (badge, scrubs, lab coat) plus on-screen studies converts skepticism into trust, and DHT gives the viewer a nameable villain their own doctor never mentioned. The dose-math and packaging callouts turn our label into the proof.

1.name: Stitch-react to the GLP-1 hair-loss lament
1.hook: Opens on the stitched clip: a woman lifts her thinning ponytail to a trending sad song, caption 'Unfortunately after a year of being on a GLP1 this is my hair — tried different vitamins nothing helps'; cut to the creator reacting — 'That video and that song, the lyrics are perfect' — then a warm…
1.why: Borrows a viral moment of raw, pre-proven pain so the creator never has to manufacture a loss story — pure validation plus answer. Single member, but it is the tier's #1 GMV video ($22.4k at 122/day) and Stitch reaction tops the Video Type leaderboard by mean revenue — thin sample, outsized signal, worth one test.

2.name: Conditional matchmaker: 'If you want longer — take this' goal/symptom router
2.hook: Creator pours/holds the supplement at 0s and delivers a rapid conditional read straight to camera: 'If you want longer hair, take this. If you want thicker hair, take this. If you want longer AND thicker, take both together'.
2.why: The conditional structure makes the viewer self-diagnose in the first 3 seconds — whichever branch they hear, the answer is the product, so every segment of the audience is addressed and routed to checkout. Product-from-0s plus a confident prescriptive read converts like a recommendation from a friend who already solved it.

2.name: Dated growth receipts: before/after journey + 'X inches by [date]' promise
2.hook: Two interlocking date-anchored openers, always with proof imagery. Lead: 'How I went from losing 50% of my hair postpartum to cutting three inches off last week because it won't stop regrowing' — hair flip up front, thinning-wet-hair 'before' photo inset.
2.why: Dated receipts convert skeptics: a concrete timeline plus visible before/after makes the outcome feel scheduled rather than hoped-for, and the calendar deadline ('by summer', 'by Christmas') creates a start-today urgency no discount is needed for.
2.sound: me va a costar — Kevin Kaarl

2.name: 'Extension allegations' real-hair discovery testimonial
2.hook: Creator flips, unclips or runs hands through visibly long thick hair in the first seconds and drops the discovery line: 'The miracle hair growth combo — I put my life on this', 'People keep asking where I got my extensions — this is literally my REAL hair', or the salon-authority version where a…
2.why: The hair on screen IS the proof — the accusation of fake hair ('extensions?', 'wig?') is flipped into irrefutable social proof, and the casual 'I gatekept this' reveal makes the product feel like an insider secret rather than an ad.
2.sound: Dark heavy metal with monstrous aggressive slow(1369719) — 212soundworks

2.name: Objection-killer proof demos: wig test, counterfeit warning, taste & side-effect myth-busts
2.hook: Reply-to-comment / demo openers that stage a doubt and destroy it on camera. Lead: replying to 'wig' — creator brushes her hair AGGRESSIVELY then holds the clean brush to the lens: 'Not a wig.
2.why: Every purchase objection (fake hair, fake product, bad taste, scary side effects, 'doesn't work') is answered as entertainment with on-camera proof, converting the skeptical comment-section audience that testimonials alone never close.
2.sound: Calm background music with acoustic guitar and saxophone(1288148) — ame

2.name: GLP-1 shedding rescue: audience callout + news-react
2.hook: Lead: green-screen news-react — creator points at a TODAY-show clip, 'FDA has issued a warning letter to the maker of Ozempic and Wegovy…', caption 'TOLD YA', then pivots to the side-effect supplement stack including a pumpkin seed oil pouch.
2.why: Names the audience in second one (GLP-1 users watching their hair fall out), borrows news/FDA authority for urgency, and offers a fix for the side effect without asking them to quit the drug they love — high-intent buyers with a fresh, painful problem.

2.name: Aging-men prostate & night-pee symptom checklist
2.hook: Lead: man stacks the symptoms straight at camera while doing a physical demo — 'If your prostate is swollen and you're dribbling, staining your britches… you're not getting that morning anymore' — slicing a beet against an anatomy model and holding up urine-stained boxers.
2.why: Names embarrassing symptoms out loud with crude visual metaphors, which stops the exact 45+ male scroller who has silently normalized them; symptom-stack plus mechanism gives him a no-doctor, no-shame fix.

2.name: Skit scenarios: caught-misusing-it comedy & 'are those extensions?' two-person bits
2.hook: Scripted mini-scenes. Highest-GMV pair are men's-health couple skits. The hair fleet: absurd product-misuse gags — 'This toast will grow your hair 3 inches by March 1st', 'Dylan, why are you eating hair vitamins on your toast?', 'Today she skipped reading the bottle — ma'am!' (pouring it on her…
2.why: Comedy earns the full watch and disarms ad-blindness; the gag always lands on the same beat — the hair (or the fix) is real and it came from this bottle — so entertainment converts into product proof.

3.name: Celebrity podcast-stitch reaction: 'Kourtney just admitted this on live TV'
3.hook: Lead: a bearded guy in a backwards cap reacts in his kitchen, pointing up — 'Kourtney Kardashian just said this on live TV and people are losing their shit, listen to this' — over a paparazzi photo and the caption 'It's not plastic surgery'; the product is withheld 3+ minutes while Kardashian…
3.why: Borrows a mega-celebrity's face and a 'leaked secret' curiosity gap to hold attention through a long clip-stacked education, so by the late reveal the product feels celebrity-endorsed and scientist-approved without the brand ever saying it.
3.sound: Horror piano, BGM when murder occurs(1193164) — syummacha

3.name: 'You're not fat, it's high cortisol' body-callout symptom checklist
3.hook: Lead: a med-spa nurse in a lab coat holds a syringe to camera — 'If your chin looks like this and your pooch looks like this, you're not fat, babe, you just have high cortisol' — while cartoon double-chin and belly-pooch overlays pop beside her face; the same 'if you've got this, this and this →…
3.why: It absolves the viewer ('you're not fat — it's not your fault') while diagnosing them in the first 5 seconds; naming a hidden culprit turns self-consciousness into a fixable deficiency the product resolves. Body-pointing plus cartoon overlays makes it visual and personal with no credential required.

3.name: Credentialed 'here's the right way' expert explainer + 'what nobody tells you' myth-bust
3.hook: Lead: a pharmacist in a white coat in the pharmacy aisle raises a finger — 'Here's how to take magnesium the right way. I'm a pharmacist.' — with the caption 'From a Pharmacist'.
3.why: A flashed credential (license, staff ID) plus PubMed screenshots converts a sales pitch into trusted advice, and the contrarian 'what nobody tells you / stop doing this' framing opens a curiosity gap that earns the full watch before the product resolves it.
3.sound: Cool for the summer hoodtrap by Kryd — Kryd

3.name: Bottle-in-hand from second 0: deal-drop testimonial opener
3.hook: Lead: a woman holds the bottle beside her face from second 0, mid-testimonial — 'My daughter even told me: Mom, I like your new self' — under a persistent caption 'This company is giving y'all $40.00, idk how long it will last', then rotates the Supplement Facts panel to camera.
3.why: Product-from-0s plus a life-changed testimonial removes all discovery friction, and the deal caption running the whole video gives fence-sitters a now-or-never reason while the story supplies the why; Sale/urgency openers are this tier's #1 device by revenue percentile.

3.name: Silent POV before/after: 'POV: you start taking this and this happens'
3.hook: A shirtless young guy tilts his head to show real acne breakouts in close-up under the caption 'POV: Empiezas a Tomar Magnesio y pasa esto…' — music only, no speech; at 16s the two-weeks-later clear-skin reveal, a two-capsule pinch to camera, then the bottle. 18 seconds total, $69.6k at 1,105/day.
3.why: A real, visible 'before' is an unfakeable scroll-stopper, and the silent time-jump reveal delivers proof in under 20 seconds — near-zero production effort for the highest-credibility message there is.

3.name: Doctor-patient comedy skit: the check-up that finds the real problem
3.hook: A doctor in scrubs and gloves winces while inspecting stained gloves mid-exam — 'Well, everything looks fine here… anything else I can help you with?' — under the caption 'It was because of a BIGGER PROBLEM'; the same actor plays both doctor and patient, comedic body-problem overlays punch each…
3.why: Comedy earns the watch-through, and the doctor-character frame lets the video diagnose the viewer's embarrassing symptoms without preaching — the product lands as the punchline prescription, softened by the laugh.
